items.title: Chuck Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 7, 2023
items.q: There was a part in the middle of it where I suggest people get on the Internet and try to find it, where it was like you turned into J.S. Bach for a little while.

ctx.x: Yeah he’s a cat that — that connection is very deep like that. It was from the first time we played, we both recognized that, I mean culturally very different upbringings but the improv thing, the freedom improv thing just jelled with us.

There was a part in the middle of it where I suggest people get on the Internet and try to find it, where it was like you turned into J.S. Bach for a little while. It was sort of a contrapuntal two thing. But going back to the wrong note business, and I wish I could think of a better term than wrong — unintended perhaps. If you’re playing with other people, bass and guitar especially, and they’re playing the changes, do you play differently than if you were playing the same song but by yourself? © Fillius Jazz…

Yeah. I do. But, because we’re following a script. But you know that’s interesting I’m just thinking are there any wrong notes, yes there are. The bass player could play — there’s mistakes but in looking at your question, depending on these musicians, so you’re following the script but if you still start — you start pushing it around all the musicians will follow the improv you know. So it does have — it still has that same freedom, you’re taking a little bit more of a risk by pushing outside the boundaries of…
